insight.title: Why Car Speedometers Start at Zero
insight.subtitle: This design quirk serves as a constant, quiet reminder of the psychological power of simplicity in mechanical engineering.

sections.text: When you glance at your dashboard, the needle almost always rests at a dead stop. While it seems logical, this choice isn’t dictated by the physics of the engine, but by human perception.

Early engineers discovered that if a gauge began at a non-zero number, drivers experienced "cognitive friction." The brain struggles to intuitively process speed if the scale doesn't align with the concept of stillness.

By anchoring the needle at zero, manufacturers created a universal language of motion. It provides an immediate, subconscious visual confirmation that the vehicle is truly at rest before you even engage the gear.
Zero is the only place where motion begins to make sense.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

Iran launched strikes against Kuwait and Bahrain early Wednesday. The attacks expanded Tehran's targets as it continues attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait’s military said it faced a wave of incoming drones targeting Ali Al Salem Air Base, which hosts United States forces. In Bahrain, missile alerts sounded twice before sunrise and air defense batteries fired after blasts were heard. From the war's start on February twenty-eighth to an April eighth ceasefire, Iran launched more than 1200 drones and missiles at Kuwait and over 700 at Bahrain, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies. Meanwhile, the United States aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Middle East. It sailed alongside the USS George Washington, bringing the total number of carriers in the region to three.

Nvidia has stopped shipping its Hopper data centre chips to China despite receiving United States government approval last year. Interim chief executive Colette Kress said the company sold two billion four hundred million dollars worth of licensed Hopper products to China in the third quarter. Kress did not elaborate on why shipments ended. The announcement followed a Trump administration move to further restrict China's access to advanced artificial intelligence chips. New rules from the United States Commerce Department target overseas data centres and chip smuggling into China. They cover shipments to Southeast Asian countries including Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

The dollar held steady near a nineteen-month high on November eighteenth as United States economic data supported the case for interest rate hikes. Data on November seventeenth showed United States retail sales increased moderately in October. The dollar index rose point zero six percent to 103.67. Traders are pricing in a 95.7 percent chance that the Federal Reserve will raise its key rate by 25 basis points in December, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Odds of a 50 basis point increase fell to 4.3 percent from 13.5 percent a month ago. Japanese data on November eighteenth showed exports rose to a record monthly value in October.

The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history has killed more than 5,500 people, according to the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Health Ministry. Emergency restrictions designed to contain the virus have made it harder for farmers to work and vendors to sell produce, according to the United Nations World Food Program. Over the past five months, 2,300,000 people have slipped into crisis levels of hunger in Congolese provinces. Women make up 60 percent of Ebola infections in Congo. This outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, has killed seven out of 10 infected children under the age of five, compared with roughly three in 10 adults, according to Unicef. The World Food Program has raised less than a quarter of the 214 million dollars it says is needed over the next six months.

Intercontinental Exchange launched a tool on Tuesday that estimates the risk of United States data-center projects being delayed or halted. The tool evaluates permitting records, electricity and water costs, local economic conditions, and mortgage-market data across more than 3,100 United States counties. The Intercontinental Exchange said its disruption model achieved 77 percent accuracy. The launch follows United States midterm elections in which Democrats gained control of both chambers of Congress. Democratic lawmakers have proposed pausing new data-center construction until Congress adopts safeguards covering utility costs and environmental damage.

The Trump administration plans to press ahead with efforts to block imports of Chinese data centre equipment despite pushback from Amazon, Google, Meta, and other United States technology companies. The Federal Communications Commission is seeking to ban United States imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers over national security concerns. Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave, and Cisco joined Microsoft in a meeting with White House officials earlier this year to oppose the measure. China boasts two-thirds of the global market for optical transceivers, according to Counterpoint Research. Chinese firms Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight dominate global supply, counting top American companies as customers.

Next, Xi Jinping urges South Korea to cooperate with China on artificial intelligence and supply chains.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is scheduled for November eighteen to nineteen, twenty twenty-six, in Shenzhen, China. Chinese President Xi Jinping is hosting the summit, which will focus on regional trade, artificial intelligence, and supply chains. High-stakes meetings are expected, including one between US President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on November nineteen.

Winter rains have flooded makeshift shelters in Gaza and destroyed scarce food supplies. Shaun Hughes, the World Food Programme country director for Palestine, said that people burn rubbish to cook, but now the rubbish is wet. Karl Baker, regional crisis coordinator for the UN International Organization for Migration, said that more than one point seven million Gazans remain displaced and one point four million face acute hunger.

The Pentagon is rushing to build more Patriot missiles, but it faces a shortage of a carbonized rayon fabric. Only one approved product of this kind exists, made by Park Aerospace at its Kansas factory using fabric supplied by the French rocket maker ArianeGroup. Brian Shore, the chief executive of Park Aerospace, said that Ariane is a French company that cannot be bullied.

Intel has let workers go in another round of job cuts led by CEO Lip-Bu Tan. Employees shared on social media about being affected in the global IT workforce. Intel employed eighty-one thousand one hundred people at the end of September, down from eighty-five thousand one hundred at the end of twenty twenty-five.

The four hundred largest data centers in the United States produced more carbon dioxide in a year than Denmark, according to a Harvard University study published Monday. Researchers looked at four hundred and three data centers between May twenty twenty-four and April twenty twenty-five. They estimated that electricity use produced about twenty-eight point three million tons of carbon dioxide.

The United States earned a D-plus for its preterm birth rate yet again. This comes from the latest March of Dimes report card, using data from the National Center for Health Statistics.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

When you glance at your car dashboard, the speedometer needle almost always rests at zero. That dead stop is not dictated by engine physics, but by human perception. Early engineers found that if a gauge began at a non-zero number, drivers experienced cognitive friction. The brain struggles to process speed if the scale does not align with stillness. Anchoring the needle at zero creates a universal language of motion. It gives a subconscious visual confirmation that the vehicle is at rest before you drive. Zero is the place where motion begins to make sense. What other daily designs rely purely on psychology rather than math?

Thanks for listening to the Sift Daily Briefing, and we will see you tomorrow.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is our full analysis of today's major global news.

Why is Iran expanding its attacks across the Persian Gulf? Tehran has launched strikes against Kuwait and Bahrain, pushing the conflict into new areas. 

To understand how we got here, we have to look back at the Middle East war. That war began on February twenty-eighth when the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran. Outright fighting has mostly subsided. But a peace deal has not been reached. The United States continues to blockade Iranian ports, which cuts off its oil exports and damages its economy. The Strait of Hormuz has become the main focus of this stalemated war. The strait is a narrow water passage that is a key route for oil and gas shipments. The U.S. military works to protect ships passing through the waterway in defiance of Iran's attempts to close it. Iran has fought back with a guerrilla campaign to disrupt traffic by any means necessary. From the war's start to an April eighth ceasefire, Iran launched over twelve hundred drones and missiles at Kuwait, and over seven hundred targeting Bahrain, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, a London-based think tank. Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet. Both nations have suffered damage to power plants, desalination facilities, and oil infrastructure. 

The situation changed when U.S. forces carried out a series of quiet strikes on Qeshm Island, which is Iran's largest island. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which is Iran's powerful military branch, has used Qeshm Island to launch drones and missiles. On Tuesday, an Iranian attack set ablaze a gas tanker named the Tara Gas, which was traveling through the strait off the coast of Oman. Authorities rescued twenty-four crew members, but one Indian mariner remained missing. 

In today's news, Iran launched strikes against Kuwait and Bahrain. Kuwait's military said it faced a wave of incoming drones targeting Ali Al Salem Air Base, which hosts U.S. forces. Kuwait did not immediately report any damage. In Bahrain, missile alerts sounded twice before sunrise, and blasts were heard as air defense batteries fired. Bahrain's armed forces said they intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks, while the Revolutionary Guards said they targeted a U.S.-operated radar system at Sheikh Isa Air Base. The U.S. military moved the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt into the region. This brought the number of U.S. carrier strike groups to three, alongside the George Washington, the George H.W. Bush, and the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer. 

This is happening now because the strikes follow an American attack on Qeshm Island, and come ahead of an unprecedented trilateral summit between President Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts. 

For the listener, this means the war remains unstable, though risk analyst Andreas Krieg notes it is a deliberate testing of boundaries rather than a full return to full-scale warfare. As you follow this story next, watch whether regional diplomacy at the upcoming summit manages to cool the fighting, or if more U.S. and Iranian strikes follow.

Now let us turn to the global technology sector, where U.S. export rules are shifting the market for artificial intelligence hardware.

Why has Nvidia stopped shipping certain AI chips to China? The company is halting shipments of its Hopper data centre processors despite earlier U.S. government approval to sell them.

To understand this move, we look at Nvidia's history of selling advanced computer chips. Nvidia is the world's leading supplier of chips used to power artificial intelligence. For years, the company spent time lobbying the U.S. government for permission to sell its powerful processors to Chinese customers. Its former chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, was the loudest advocate for these exports, and built a strong personal relationship with President Donald Trump. While the Trump administration refused to approve Nvidia's advanced Blackwell chips for sale to China, it did clear the sale of H200 processors. These processors belong to the Hopper generation, which is two generations behind Nvidia's leading Rubin family of chips. 

The situation changed following a leadership crisis at Nvidia. Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive last week after disclosing multiple extramarital affairs. One affair involved a woman currently under investigation by the U.S. government for potentially aiding China's spy agency and possibly helping smuggle chips to China. Beijing has denied any attempt to spy on Huang. Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first chair, and the company named Colette Kress as interim chief executive. 

In today's news, Kress announced during an earnings call that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre products to China. The company sold two billion four hundred million dollars worth of these licensed products to China in the third quarter. Kress did not explain why the shipments are ending. The announcement comes just a day after the Trump administration moved to further restrict China's access to advanced AI chips. The new U.S. Commerce Department rules target overseas data centres and smuggling efforts in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power. Despite the halt to Chinese shipments and leadership changes, Nvidia projected strong financial results. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of one hundred thirty billion dollars, which was higher than average analyst estimates. 

This is happening now because the U.S. government is tightening export curbs and increasing scrutiny ahead of President Donald Trump's visit to China for talks with President Xi Jinping. 

For the listener, this means a major supplier is pulling back from its biggest overseas market due to growing national security pressures. Nvidia has also formed a new board committee dedicated to national security and export controls. As you watch this story next, look for how Nvidia's next permanent chief executive navigates these export rules, and whether restrictions tighten further.

Next, we look at currency markets and what they tell us about the American economy.

Why is the U.S. dollar holding near a nineteen-month high? Strong American economic data and comments from Federal Reserve officials have reinforced expectations for interest rate hikes.

To understand how currency values work, we look at the role of the Federal Reserve, which is the central bank of the United States. When the U.S. economy grows strongly and demand for goods rises, the Fed uses interest rates to control inflation, which is the rising cost of goods and services. Higher interest rates make a currency more attractive to global investors, which raises its value compared to other currencies. Over recent months, the U.S. economy has shown strong domestic demand, leading central bank officials to consider raising borrowing costs. 

The situation changed when a fresh batch of economic reports arrived on November seventeenth and eighteenth. These reports measured retail sales, import prices, and manufacturing data, giving economists a clear look at how fast consumers are spending money. 

In today's news, data showed U.S. retail sales increased moderately by zero point two percent in October, matching expectations. Import prices climbed one point one percent in October, which was higher than the expected zero point seven percent increase. The dollar index rose zero point zero six percent to one hundred three point sixty-seven, staying near a nineteen-month high touched overnight. Traders are now pricing in a ninety-five point seven percent chance that the Fed will raise its key interest rate by twenty-five basis points in December, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Meanwhile, other global currencies moved in response. The yen held its ground after Bank of Japan governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated the need to tighten policy further, and Japanese data showed exports rose to a record monthly value in October. The Australian dollar fell to a ten-month low ahead of a key jobs report. 

This is happening now because recent inflation data and consumer spending numbers have given central bank officials the evidence they need to debate further monetary tightening. 

For the listener, this means borrowing costs in the United States could soon go higher, which affects everything from mortgages to global trade. Henry Russell, an economist for ANZ, argues that the strength of domestic demand warrants a decisive policy response from the Fed. As you watch what happens next, keep an eye on the upcoming release of the Federal Reserve meeting minutes and future speeches from central bank leaders to see if the expected December rate hike becomes reality.

That economic strength directly impacts global health efforts, where a severe hunger crisis is now making a deadly disease outbreak even harder to control.

Why is the latest Ebola outbreak becoming even more dangerous for sick people? Growing hunger in East Africa is increasing the risk of death for infected patients. Ebola is a serious virus that causes violent sickness and high fever. It spreads through direct physical contact with body fluids or human corpses. For decades, regions in Central and East Africa have fought recurring virus outbreaks. In local Congolese culture, women care for sick relatives and perform traditional burial rites. These caring tasks make women far more likely to catch the virus from others. During past outbreaks, international aid groups managed hundreds of food points and care centers. Food rations gave sick bodies necessary nutrients to resist infection. Free food also gave families a strong reason to isolate for twenty-one days after exposure. While delivering food, health workers countered rumors and taught people how to prevent infection. But Congolese authorities recently introduced strict rules to contain the spreading virus. They prohibited travel between villages and placed strict limits on local fishing activities. These restrictions stopped farmers from working fields and vendors from selling produce. In one Congolese town, a food seller named Ketra Biira closed her market stall. She got stuck at home with almost nothing to feed her young children. She said some vendors even refuse cash because they fear money carries the virus. Another thirty-year-old Congolese fisherman named Asifiwe Chantalia sneaked into Uganda to find food. Ugandan police arrested him in Echuya National Park and plan to send him back. Today, the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history sweeps across the region. Congo's Health Ministry says Ebola has already killed more than five thousand five hundred people. Almost all of these reported deaths occurred within the Democratic Republic of Congo. The United Nations World Food Program says two point three million people entered crisis hunger. That hunger surge happened over five months in Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu. Unicef reports that women make up sixty percent of Ebola cases in Congo. Unicef also says this rare strain kills seven out of ten infected young children. That compares to roughly three out of ten adults who die from the virus. World Food Program official David Stevenson says his agency lacks dangerous levels of money. The agency raised less than a quarter of two hundred fourteen million dollars needed. Meanwhile, charity CARE International closed about one thousand nutrition centers across Congo. The World Health Organization said eleven patients in Ituri received no food for a week. Movement limits leave people isolated, forcing them to choose between hunger or disease. An ongoing Islamic State insurgency also disrupts farming and delays crucial aid deliveries. The World Food Program warns life-threatening hunger could reach four point two million people early next year. Listeners can watch if international donors step up funding to reopen nutrition centers.

Now let us turn to technology infrastructure in the United States.

How can investors know if a new computer facility might face construction delays? A financial exchange operator made a software model to predict local project delays. Data centers are large facilities filled with thousands of running computer servers. These computer warehouses power artificial intelligence software and complex internet services. Operating these servers requires large amounts of electrical power and cooling water. Over recent years, technology companies rushed to build new facilities across the country. But local communities began opposing new construction projects near their homes. Residents expressed deep concerns about rising electricity bills, heavy water usage, and pollution. Local planning boards began delaying permit approvals or denying official land development rights. These local political disputes created unexpected financial delays for infrastructure investors. Then, Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in November twenty twenty-six. Democratic lawmakers soon proposed pausing new data center builds across the nation. On Tuesday, New York Stock Exchange owner Intercontinental Exchange launched a risk tool. This tool estimates the risk of data center projects being delayed or halted. It analyzes local permitting records, electricity costs, water costs, economic conditions, and mortgage data. Before building, companies need official town permits, which local boards can delay. The software evaluates these local factors across more than three thousand one hundred United States counties. Intercontinental Exchange trained the software model on thousands of past permitting and project outcomes. The company says its disruption model achieved seventy-seven percent accuracy in tests. ICE executive Larry Lawrence said capital moves faster than local permitting and community consensus. He explained that this gap has now become a material financial risk. Meanwhile, Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez proposed pausing data center expansions. She urged Congress to adopt safeguards covering utility costs, environmental damage, and community oversight. Political scrutiny increased after federal elections strengthened lawmakers focused on power consumption and pollution. Local opposition and national politics now threaten the rapid expansion of infrastructure needed for artificial intelligence. Investors could use this software to spot counties where community opposition is high. But computer models alone cannot stop Congress from passing strict federal build limits. Listeners should watch whether lawmakers introduce bills that pause new facility construction nationwide.

Next, national security concerns are hitting computer hardware supply chains in Washington.

Why is the United States moving to block key Chinese data center imports? Washington officials fear Chinese network hardware creates national security risks for domestic computing infrastructure. Optical transceivers are small electronic components used inside data centers. They allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light. China boasts two-thirds of the global market for optical transceivers, according to Counterpoint Research. Chinese companies like Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight dominate global supply. The Pentagon recently added Zhongji Innolight to its list of Chinese military-backed companies. Top American technology hyperscalers count these Chinese vendors among their main suppliers. In August, reports revealed the Federal Communications Commission sought to ban new Chinese transceiver models. China hawks in Washington warned Beijing could use transceivers to steal data or disrupt services. Earlier this year, Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave, and Cisco joined Microsoft in a White House meeting. Corporate executives pushed back against the proposed import ban during these private talks. They told White House officials American firms could need up to a decade to comply. According to a report by the Foundation for American Innovation, domestic technology lacks scale. American firms Coherent and Lumentum produce competing tech but cannot match Chinese production scale. Industry leaders also warned that China might retaliate by banning exports of indium phosphide. Indium phosphide is a critical mineral needed for American firms to make transceivers. Despite this heavy tech lobbying, three sources say the measure is moving forward. A White House official declined to comment on lobbying or progress. But the official said past FCC bans resulted in billions in investments and thousands of jobs. Over the last year, the FCC successfully barred Chinese drones, robots, power inverters, and routers. Calls for action grew after revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. That scandal put a spotlight on Nvidia AI chips being smuggled into China without Commerce Department action. Standardizing on domestic suppliers could increase production costs and delay construction timelines for tech giants. Listeners should watch whether the FCC formally enacts the ban and if Beijing retaliates with mineral export limits.

Next, Chinese President Xi Jinping is urging South Korea to cooperate on artificial intelligence and supply chains.

Why are top world leaders meeting in China for an economic summit? President Xi Jinping is hosting twenty-one economies to discuss trade, supply chains, and artificial intelligence.

In nineteen eighty-nine, Asia-Pacific nations formed an economic group called APEC. This group is not a trade bloc. Decisions are made voluntarily by consensus. Today, these economies include thirty-six percent of the world population. In twenty twenty-five, they created sixty-one point four trillion dollars in total economic output. They produced half of all global goods exports, worth thirteen point two trillion dollars. China hosted this summit in Shanghai in two thousand one. China hosted it again in Beijing in twenty fourteen. Relations between the United States and China worsened over trade disagreements. Last year, President Donald Trump and Xi met in South Korea. They created a functional trade truce known as the Busan Agreement. The United States lowered tariffs, and China loosened controls on rare earths.

Now, China is hosting the summit again after twelve years.

The event runs from November eighteen to nineteen, twenty twenty-six, in Shenzhen. Shenzhen is a major technology hub, letting China showcase its innovation. President Trump arrives after visiting Manila for the ASEAN summit. In Manila, Trump meets leaders from the Quad group. That group includes the United States, India, Australia, and Japan. These democratic nations work together to balance power against China. Trump will also sign a trade deal with Thailand. Then, Trump meets Xi in Shenzhen on November nineteen. They want to extend their trade truce past January ten, twenty twenty-seven. Washington wants rare earths, while Beijing wants relief from economic pressure. Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold their first joint summit. Trump wants to discuss denuclearization, Iran, and Ukraine. Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will not attend this gathering. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will also meet Xi. Canada agreed to take forty-nine thousand Chinese electric vehicles at a six point one percent tariff. This replaced an extra one hundred percent tax. China eased trade barriers on Canadian canola and seafood. Relations had hurt after Canada arrested Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou in twenty eighteen. China then detained two Canadians. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi might also speak with Xi. Ties worsened after she said a Chinese attack on Taiwan threatens Japan. Tokyo has not confirmed her attendance as of November fifteen.

This summit is happening because the current trade truce expires in January.

The meetings could decide if major nations can keep trade moving smoothly. Watch to see whether Trump and Xi officially extend their trade deal.

Now, let us turn to a growing humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

Why are living conditions getting worse for families in Gaza? Winter rains flooded makeshift camps, destroying scarce food supplies and tents.

Conflict in Gaza displaced over one point seven million people from their homes. Families moved into makeshift tent camps across the region. Shaun Hughes is the Palestine country director for the World Food Programme. He explained that Israeli military control covers nearly seventy percent of Gaza. That control leaves people almost no space to grow food. Fishing in the sea is prohibited and life-threatening. Unemployment in Gaza is over eighty percent. People rely almost entirely on aid agencies for survival. One in four Gaza households is headed by a woman. Widows and women with missing husbands face unimaginable hardship alone. Aid agencies worked for months to prepare camps for cold weather. Teams dug drainage channels and reinforced dirt pathways. They filled old flour bags with sand to block water.

Heavy winter rains arrived and flooded thousands of temporary shelters.

Hughes warned that rain and sewage destroyed food stored in tents. Most people burn trash to cook, but now the trash is wet. Karl Baker coordinates crisis response for the International Organization for Migration. He said one day of rain damaged or destroyed tens of thousands of shelters. A sand bank collapsed a week ago, killing at least five people. Two children died in tent fires while families tried to stay warm. About one point four million Gazans face acute hunger. The World Food Programme reduced hot meals from one daily to one every two days. Aid groups need nine million dollars for basic flood prevention and winter supplies. Over one hundred thousand tents sit in Egypt waiting for delivery approval. Israel controls imports through strict bureaucracy at border checkpoints. Baker works with Israel's Coordination of Government Activities in the Territories. This agency checks all incoming equipment for security rules. Clearance takes a long time and involves heavy bureaucracy. For example, tent poles wider than thirty-eight millimeters are usually rejected. In the decade before twenty twenty-two, small defense businesses shrank by forty percent. Many manufacturing jobs shifted overseas. Boeing makes the steering seekers, and L3Harris makes the rocket motors. The newest Patriot model is called the PAC-3 MSE. Over seventy percent of second-tier suppliers also supply another system called Thaad. If one supplier fails, multiple missile programs face delays.

That estimate comes from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The Pentagon signed a seven-year agreement with Lockheed Martin to accelerate production. L3Harris is also working to qualify a second source for rayon. The Pentagon stated that it is continually working on supply chain resilience.

Global demand drained missile stockpiles faster than factories could replace them.

The company has let more workers go in another round of cuts. 

Intel is a huge technology company that makes computer chips. These are the small electronic parts that power computers and phones. For years, Intel was the top chipmaker in the world. 

Then things got harder. Other companies caught up in making chips for artificial intelligence. Intel also had troubles making its own chips. 

The business started losing money and falling behind. So Intel brought in a new leader named Lip-Bu Tan. He is the chief executive officer, which means he is the top boss. 

His job is to fix the company and make it make money again. To do that, Tan started a big plan to lower costs. He wants to cut layers of management and get rid of projects that do not make money.

An Intel spokesperson spoke about the cuts. The spokesperson said the company wants to become a more focused and efficient company. 

The spokesperson added that Intel continually assesses its workforce to ensure priorities and resources are aligned. Intel did not disclose how many employees were affected or identify the teams involved. 

These cuts are happening now because the company has been trying to revive its business for years. The job cuts add to a lengthy restructuring at the United States chipmaker. 

Intel employed 81,100 people at the end of September. That is down from 85,100 at the end of twenty twenty-five, according to company filings. 

The headcount has fallen sharply since twenty twenty-four. That was when Intel announced plans to cut more than 15,000 jobs, or about 15 percent of its workforce, under then-chief executive officer Pat Gelsinger. 

For you, this shows how fast the tech industry changes when a company misses a big trend like artificial intelligence. You can watch to see if Tan's cost-cutting plan finally helps Intel catch up to its rivals. 

Now, onto our next story. How much pollution do large data centers make? 

A new study shows that the 400 largest data centers in the United States put more heat-trapping gas in the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did. 

Data centers are huge buildings full of computers that store information and run the internet and artificial intelligence. They use massive amounts of electricity to run and stay cool. 

Most of that electricity comes from burning fossil fuels like coal and gas. Burning fossil fuels creates carbon dioxide, which is a gas that warms up the planet. 

As more people use the internet and artificial intelligence, tech companies keep building more data centers. That makes their electricity consumption rise. 

The electricity consumption rose 240 percent between twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-five, according to a report by a group called Climate Action Against Disinformation. 

Now, this situation has turned into big news because of a new study and a global meeting. Harvard University researchers looked at 403 of the largest United States data centers between May twenty twenty-four and April twenty twenty-five. 

They found that electricity use by the centers produced around 28.3 million tons of carbon dioxide. That is about 25.7 million metric tons. 

More than half of their 82 terawatt hours of electricity use came from fossil fuels. That amount of electricity is enough to power nearly 7 million homes for a year. 

Study senior author Francesca Dominici said the emissions estimate is two to three times what previous studies had shown. She is a Harvard biostatistics professor. 

She added that plans for 2,000 more data centers make that quantity more worrisome for the future. Meanwhile, negotiators at the United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, launched a voluntary pledge on Monday. 

The pledge asks companies and countries to power data centers with clean energy. It also asks them to be more open about their power and water consumption and emissions. 

United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell spoke at the launch. He said claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now. 

Some people are hopeful that artificial intelligence can also help solve climate problems. Former United States Vice President Al Gore said he is less concerned about emissions from artificial intelligence than others. 

He pointed to a study predicting advanced artificial intelligence could help reduce greenhouse gases by 6 to 9 percent by 2030. Caleb Max is president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association. 

He said artificial intelligence will solve energy usage issues and make lives better. But Philip Newell, a spokesman for Climate Action Against Disinformation, was skeptical. 

He said companies are selling hope while hiding the harms. To help reduce the impact, some companies want to capture waste heat from data centers. 

That heat can be used to warm nearby homes and businesses. The International Energy Agency estimates data centers could provide enough heat for around 10 percent of European homes by 2030. 

For you, this means your use of technology has a hidden environmental cost that governments are starting to track closely. You can watch to see if tech companies actually sign the new clean energy pledge and change how they build future data centers. 

Now, onto our final news story. How did the United States do on premature births? 

The United States earned a grade of D+ for its preterm birth rate, according to the latest report card from the March of Dimes. 

Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health problems. 

Before we go, here is your thought for the day. 

When you look at your car dashboard, the speed needle almost always rests at zero. That seems normal, but it is actually a clever trick of human psychology. 

Early engineers found a big problem when gauges started at a non-zero number. Drivers experienced cognitive friction. 

That means the brain struggles to process speed if the scale does not start at stillness. So engineers anchored the needle at zero to create a universal language of motion. 

It gives you instant proof that the car is truly stopped before you even shift gears. Zero is the quiet starting point where all motion begins to make sense. 

It makes you wonder what other everyday things are designed around how our brains work instead of simple math. 

Thank you for spending time with us today on Sift In-Depth. We hope you take these thoughts with you, and we look forward to exploring more stories together next time.
